title: The Rocket Factory Is Being Rebuilt From Scratch
subtitle: AI-driven design, orbital manufacturing, and in-space construction are dismantling traditional rocket production simultaneously — from three directions, at three different stages of maturity.
summary: Traditional rocket manufacturing — design over years, test, fail, redesign, repeat — is being dismantled simultaneously from three directions. AI closes the design loop in weeks instead of years. Metal 3D printers build flight-ready engines in days. And orbital manufacturing is moving from demonstration to clinical pipeline. Each layer is at a different stage of maturity. Each has a different investment profile. None is fully priced.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: The way rockets, space hardware, and advanced materials get built is being reinvented across three layers simultaneously — AI-driven design, orbital manufacturing, and in-space construction. This is not a future capability. It is running in production facilities today.
THE ROCKET FACTORY IS BEING REBUILT FROM SCRATCH

Traditional rocket manufacturing is a slow, expensive, iterative process — design over years, test, fail, redesign, repeat, at a cost that has historically made the barrier to entry prohibitive. That model is being dismantled simultaneously from three directions. Each layer is at a different stage of maturity. Each has a different investment profile. None is fully priced.
LAYER 1 — DESIGN AND PRINT: AI CLOSES THE LOOP

The new way to build a rocket engine: an AI model encodes the physics and generates a complete, production-ready design in minutes. A metal 3D printer builds it in days. The iteration loop that used to cost years and hundreds of millions now takes weeks. Rocket Lab prints a flight-ready Rutherford engine every few days at its dedicated Long Beach AM facility. Stoke Space ordered five Additive Industries MetalFab 420K printers in November 2025 for production-scale manufacturing of its Nova reusable rocket.

SpaceX's Raptor 3 reflects the endpoint of this trend: nearly all external plumbing eliminated, cooling channels printed directly into the engine body as integrated monolithic components using GRCop-42, a copper alloy developed with NASA — hundreds of weld failure points removed from a single engine.

One geopolitical data point worth tracking: LegendSpace, a Beijing-based AI rocket engine startup founded in January 2026, raised $29.5 million in angel funding. Its Prime platform links AI-driven design, multi-physics simulation, additive manufacturing, and hot-fire testing into a closed loop it claims can compress engine iteration cycles to around two weeks. This is a competitive signal that this approach is now running inside the PRC space ecosystem.

Investor Consideration: High-rate AM engine production is proven at the small-to-medium launch vehicle scale. Orbital-class thrust — the kind that powers heavy-lift rockets — requires solving turbomachinery sealing, material fatigue, and transient startup at a scale an order of magnitude larger. That milestone remains ahead. The companies that close that gap first will define the economics of the next decade of heavy lift.

title: The Launch Stack Is Being Rebuilt From the Top Down
subtitle: The Pentagon added an orbital transfer vehicle company as a national security prime contractor for the first time in NSSL history — four days before a NASA-backed cryogenic refueling demo rolled to the pad.
summary: On July 7, the U.S. Space Force awarded Impulse Space and Relativity Federal positions on the NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 contract, expanding the eligible provider pool to seven companies. Impulse Space — an orbital transfer vehicle developer, not a rocket manufacturer — became the first upper-stage company to hold prime contractor status in NSSL history. The Space Force is no longer just buying rides to orbit. It's buying delivery to destination.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: The Pentagon rewired its launch program on July 7, adding an orbital transfer vehicle company as a national security prime contractor for the first time in NSSL history — and four days later, a NASA-backed cryogenic refueling demo rolled to the pad. The infrastructure layer of the next space economy is being assembled in real time.
THE LAUNCH STACK IS BEING REBUILT FROM THE TOP DOWN

For two decades, the business of getting national security payloads to orbit looked like a duopoly. SpaceX and United Launch Alliance divided the missions, split the revenue, and absorbed most of the risk tolerance the Pentagon was willing to extend. The National Security Space Launch program was built around that reality: expensive, reliable, and deliberately limited to a short list of proven providers. That architecture has now formally ended.

On July 7, the U.S. Space Force awarded Impulse Space and Relativity Federal positions on the NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 contract, a $5.6 billion indefinite-delivery vehicle that routes risk-tolerant national security launches to commercially capable providers. The additions expanded the eligible pool to seven companies — SpaceX, ULA, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab (NASDAQ: RKLB), Stoke Space, and the two newcomers — and the Space Force confirmed it intends to reopen the competition annually.

What makes the Impulse Space selection structurally significant isn't the company's name — it's the job description. Impulse is an orbital transfer vehicle developer, not a rocket manufacturer. Its Helios upper stage is designed to take payloads from low Earth orbit to geosynchronous orbit in under a day, riding partner medium-lift vehicles rather than building its own first stage. In the entire history of NSSL, prime contractors have been launch vehicle operators. Impulse Space is the first upper-stage company to hold that designation.

The Space Force is no longer just buying rides to orbit — it's buying delivery to destination. On July 11, a Rocket Lab Electron rocket lifted off carrying LOXSAT, a NASA-funded payload built by Eta Space to validate eleven cryogenic fluid management technologies over nine months in LEO: zero-loss liquid oxygen storage, propellant gauging in microgravity, automated tank pressure control, and transfer mechanics. These are the foundational building blocks of orbital refueling at scale.

Investor Consideration: Rocket Lab (RKLB) holds a dual position in this story — as a launch provider and as the vehicle that put the refueling demonstrator on orbit. The orbital transfer vehicle category is almost entirely private. The most direct public exposure to the infrastructure layer being built here runs through the defense primes and the handful of launch companies with public tickers.

title: The Thruster Race: How In-Space Propulsion Became the Space Economy's Next Bottleneck
subtitle: Most satellite investors can name the rocket that gets a spacecraft to orbit. Almost none can name the thruster that keeps it there. That gap is closing fast.
summary: Every satellite has two propulsion problems: how to get there and how to stay. The first problem — launch — has attracted billions in investment and several public companies. The second problem, maneuvering and station-keeping once on orbit, has been invisible to generalist investors. That is starting to change. Electric propulsion has become the standard for constellation station-keeping, and the supply chain behind it is tightening in ways the market hasn't priced.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: Most satellite investors can name the rocket that gets a spacecraft to orbit — almost none can name the thruster that keeps it there. That gap is closing fast, and the money moving into in-space propulsion is worth understanding before the market prices it in.
THE THRUSTER RACE: HOW IN-SPACE PROPULSION BECAME THE SPACE ECONOMY'S NEXT BOTTLENECK

Every satellite ever built has two propulsion problems: how to get there and how to stay. The first problem — launch — has attracted billions of investment dollars and several public companies. The second problem, maneuvering and station-keeping once on orbit, has mostly been invisible to generalist investors. That is starting to change.

CU Aerospace, a private company most people outside the satellite industry have never heard of, builds two thruster technologies with no equivalent in the catalog of names most space investors follow. The first is the Fiber-fed Pulsed Plasma Thruster — which runs on a spool of solid PTFE (essentially Teflon) and requires no pressurized tanks, no valves, no hazardous propellant handling. The second, Monofilament Vaporization Propulsion, heats the same class of solid polymer fiber to generate electrothermal thrust for orbital maneuvers. Both systems flew on CU Aerospace's DUPLEX CubeSat, deployed from the International Space Station in December 2025.

DARPA has selected CU Aerospace to develop an airbreathing thruster for very-low-Earth-orbit operations — a regime where conventional thrusters cannot function because there is barely enough atmosphere to poison them but enough to create drag. This is the frontier of in-space propulsion: no pressure vessels, solid inert propellant, scalable pulse-by-pulse precision, and multi-year mission life with no refueling.

Electric propulsion — primarily Hall thrusters and gridded ion drives — has become the standard for constellation station-keeping. Every one of SpaceX's roughly 7,000 Starlink satellites uses a krypton Hall thruster. OneWeb, Amazon Kuiper, and every new LEO constellation follows the same architecture. The supply chain behind Hall thruster propellant and the specialized magnets and ceramics inside the thrusters is tightening in ways the market hasn't yet priced into the component manufacturers.

Investor Consideration: The investable story sits one tier up the power curve from the private developers. The public names with meaningful exposure to in-space propulsion are primarily the defense electronics and advanced materials companies supplying the magnet and ceramic components inside Hall thrusters — not the thruster integrators themselves, most of which remain private.

title: The Line Nobody Read in the S-1
subtitle: SpaceX buried Starfall in its S-1 as a single bullet point. Two weeks after the IPO, it flew. The reentry market just got its most consequential entrant.
summary: When SpaceX filed its S-1 in May, the financial press focused on Starlink's $4.4 billion operating income. Buried in the filing was a single bullet point referencing in-orbit manufacturing capabilities. On June 23 — eleven days after SPCX began trading — that bullet point flew. Starfall is SpaceX's uncrewed reentry capsule: 3.1 meters wide, 2,100 kilograms, carrying up to 1,000 kilograms of payload back from orbit. It was recovered in the Pacific roughly 48 hours after launch.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: SpaceX buried Starfall in its S-1 as a single bullet point. Two weeks after the IPO, it flew. The reentry market just got its most consequential entrant — and the investable picture is more nuanced than the headlines suggest.
THE LINE NOBODY READ IN THE S-1

When SpaceX filed its S-1 in May, the financial press spent its energy on Starlink's $4.4 billion operating income, the Anthropic and Google compute contracts, and the $75 billion raise. Buried in the filing, almost as an afterthought, was a single bullet point referencing in-orbit manufacturing capabilities. On June 23 — eleven days after SPCX began trading — that bullet point flew.

Starfall is SpaceX's uncrewed reentry capsule: a flat disk, 3.1 meters wide, 0.75 meters tall, 2,100 kilograms, carrying up to 1,000 kilograms of payload back from orbit. It launched from Cape Canaveral at 6:53 a.m., was recovered in the Pacific, and was trucked through the Port of Long Beach by June 25 — roughly 48 hours from orbit to inspection.

The FAA's own FONSI/ROD states SpaceX's purpose directly: "enable point-to-point delivery of critical cargo through space on rapid timelines" and "create a self-sustaining commercial in-space manufacturing market by offering access to microgravity and vacuum, loiter on orbit, and safe return from orbit as a service at scale." What the coverage missed is the military layer: SpaceX treated the launch like a classified mission — no upper stage broadcast, terse post-liftoff update, no disclosure on payload, duration, or recovery results.

That secrecy pattern has context. In 2022, the Air Force Research Laboratory awarded SpaceX a $102 million contract to demonstrate point-to-point cargo delivery globally via Starship. The Pentagon's REGAL program — Rocket Experimentation for Global Agile Logistics — has explicitly framed this capability as a pathway to a program of record, meaning recurring annual defense budget line items.

Investor Consideration: The investable picture has three layers. First, SPCX itself — Starfall adds a third revenue vector alongside Starlink and Colossus compute. Second, the reentry startup ecosystem: Varda Space Industries (Series C, $329M raised, six missions launched, five successful reentries), Inversion Space, Outpost, ATMOS Space Cargo, Reditus Space — all private. Third, the in-space manufacturing supply chain, where the public exposure is thin but growing. A confirmed defense contract for Starfall would be a material new disclosure.

title: The Organs We Can't Print on Earth
subtitle: Gravity makes soft human tissue collapse before it can knit into an organ. Orbit removes that ceiling — and the companies turning that single fact into a product pipeline are split between a defense stock, a cash-strapped printer maker, and a wall of private firms you mostly can't touch.
summary: More than 100,000 people sit on the U.S. transplant waiting list, and roughly thirteen die every day waiting for an organ that never comes. The bioprinting industry spent fifteen years trying to turn this from a supply problem into a manufacturing problem. Nobody has printed a functioning organ that works on Earth — because gravity collapses soft tissue before it can bond. In microgravity, cells don't sink. Redwire printed a human knee meniscus on the ISS in 2023. Auxilium Biotechnologies has an eighty-patient clinical trial underway for a microgravity-printed nerve-repair device.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: Gravity makes soft human tissue collapse before it can knit into an organ. Orbit removes that ceiling — and the companies turning that single fact into a product pipeline are split between a defense stock, a cash-strapped printer maker, and a wall of private firms you mostly can't touch.
THE ORGANS WE CAN'T PRINT ON EARTH

Start with a number that doesn't move: more than 100,000 people sit on the U.S. transplant waiting list, and roughly thirteen of them die every day waiting for an organ that never comes. The bioprinting industry spent fifteen years trying to refile this as a manufacturing problem: print a functioning organ from the patient's own cells, and the donor queue stops being the bottleneck. Nobody has printed one that works. And the reason is physics, not biology.

Living tissue is soft. Print a three-dimensional structure from cells suspended in a watery bio-ink and gravity drags the cells down before they bond, collapsing the structure into a puddle. The terrestrial workaround is scaffolding — rigid supports or thickeners stiff enough to hold a shape — but scaffolds get in the way of the soft, vessel-rich tissue a real organ requires. In microgravity, cells don't sink and soft structures don't collapse. You can print scaffold-free.

This stopped being theoretical in the last two years. Redwire used its BioFabrication Facility aboard the ISS to print a human knee meniscus on orbit in 2023, then a live human cardiac-tissue sample returned to Earth in 2024. A private San Diego firm, Auxilium Biotechnologies, printed a batch of implantable nerve-repair devices in microgravity in roughly two hours in late 2024, and has since opened an eighty-patient pivotal clinical trial for the terrestrial version.

That trial is the detail that separates this moment from the decade of demonstrations before it: a microgravity-printed device is no longer a photograph in a press release but the upstream end of a regulated clinical pathway with patients enrolled. NASA states it plainly — on Earth bioprinting needs a support structure; on the station, tissue holds three-dimensional shape without one.

Investor Consideration: The science is outrunning the investable surface beneath it. The most advanced work sits either inside large companies where bioprinting is a rounding error, or inside private firms with no public door. The pure-play public names a previous generation of investors remember have mostly dissolved, pivoted, or shrunk. The honest version: the unmet need is enormous and verifiable, the on-orbit progress is documented, and the clean ways to own a piece of it are very few. That gap is itself the signal.

title: The Week the Lunar Economy Became Investable
subtitle: The largest IPO in history closed the same week the first infrastructure-class lunar lander rolled out of its Pittsburgh cleanroom. For the first time, the capital and the hardware arrived in the same news cycle.
summary: For years, space investors faced a timing problem. The thesis was obvious — launch costs falling, government demand rising, off-Earth infrastructure inevitable — but the addressable market kept receding just ahead of the capital. Last week, that changed. SpaceX priced at $135 per share, raised $85.7 billion, and began trading as SPCX. In the same week, Astrobotic's Griffin lander rolled out of its Pittsburgh cleanroom — the first infrastructure-class lunar lander built by a private company to reach that milestone.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: The largest IPO in history closed the same week the first infrastructure-class lunar lander rolled out of its Pittsburgh cleanroom. For the first time, the capital and the hardware arrived in the same news cycle — and the investment map just got a lot more specific.
THE WEEK THE LUNAR ECONOMY BECAME INVESTABLE

For years, space investors faced a timing problem. The thesis was obvious — launch costs falling, government demand rising, off-Earth infrastructure inevitable — but the addressable market kept receding just ahead of the capital. You could buy a satellite manufacturer or an Earth observation company, but the deeper lunar and cislunar economy lived in PowerPoint, not in portfolios. Last week, that changed in a single news cycle.

On Thursday, June 12, SpaceX (Nasdaq: SPCX) priced its IPO at $135 per share and began trading as a public company for the first time in its 24-year history. The stock opened at $150, closed its first session up 19.2% at $160.95, and continued climbing. By Monday, SPCX was trading above $177. Underwriters exercised the full greenshoe overallotment, bringing total capital raised to $85.7 billion — the largest IPO on record, more than double Saudi Aramco's $29.4 billion in 2019.

The number that matters most for SPCX investors isn't the opening price — it's what the S-1 reveals about where the money actually comes from. Starlink generated $11.4 billion in revenue in 2025 with $4.4 billion in operating income and an adjusted EBITDA margin of roughly 63%. The market is not pricing a rocket company. It is pricing satellite infrastructure with a rocket division and a two-decade runway.

The crack in the thesis is also in the S-1. Average revenue per Starlink subscriber fell from $99/month in 2023 to $66/month in Q1 2026, as SpaceX pushed into lower-income markets. Subscribers more than doubled; revenue per subscriber fell 33%. Investors who are long SPCX are making a specific bet: that Starship's commercial debut in the second half of 2026 unlocks a step-change in constellation economics before the ARPU compression becomes structurally damaging.

Investor Consideration: The first earnings report lands September 2, 2026 — the first hard price anchor for SPCX. Until then, volatility will be high: the float is limited because most shares remain with Musk and existing investors. The lunar lander milestone in the same week signals that the cislunar economy is moving from demonstration to hardware. The investment map is shifting from "will this happen" to "who wins when it does."

title: The Metal That Runs Through Everything — and China Controls 60%
subtitle: AI data centers need optical fiber. Optical fiber needs germanium. China banned exports in December 2024. Here is what that means for every satellite manufacturer.
summary: While the investment community watches the SpaceX IPO roadshow, the story that will actually shape costs for SpaceX, xAI, and every satellite manufacturer is playing out quietly in zinc smelters across China. Germanium — a byproduct of zinc refining with no viable substitute at production scale — is the dopant that gives optical fiber its ability to carry light over long distances. China controls approximately 60% of global germanium refining and banned exports to the United States in December 2024. Prices rose 200% between January 2024 and February 2026. At least one major US fiber manufacturer sold out inventory through year-end 2026.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: While the investment community watches the SpaceX IPO roadshow, the stories worth taking a closer look at are the ones that will shape costs for SpaceX, xAI, and every satellite manufacturer for the next decade — quietly, downstream, and without a single press release announcing their arrival. One of them starts in a town of 947 people in Oklahoma.
THE METAL THAT RUNS THROUGH EVERYTHING — AND CHINA CONTROLS 60%

Here is the chain of events. Follow it once and you will never look at the AI infrastructure buildout the same way. AI data centers require optical fiber. Optical fiber requires germanium — a dopant with no viable substitute at production scale that gives the glass its ability to carry light over long distances.

Germanium is not a metal you can mine directly. It comes out of zinc smelters as a byproduct, extracted from residue that most Western operators have historically discarded or stockpiled as waste. China recognized this decades ago and built the refining infrastructure to process it at scale. Today China controls approximately 60% of global germanium refining. In December 2024, Beijing banned germanium exports to the United States. Prices rose 200% between January 2024 and February 2026. At least one major US fiber manufacturer sold out its inventory through year-end 2026.
That is the chokepoint. Here is why it matters to you specifically.

Every Starlink terminal uses optical transceivers. Every ground station that connects a satellite constellation to the terrestrial internet backbone runs on fiber. The xAI Colossus data center in Memphis — and every data center like it being built to train and run AI models — depends on fiber connectivity at a scale that was not anticipated when procurement contracts were written. The supply chain disruption is already priced into fiber manufacturers. It is not yet priced into the satellite operators and AI infrastructure companies that depend on them.

The company in that Oklahoma town of 947 people is one of fewer than a dozen US facilities capable of processing germanium-bearing feedstock into usable product. Its capacity constraints are now a national security concern. The Defense Production Act has been invoked. None of this has produced a single new tonne of refined germanium yet.

Investor Consideration: The near-term winners are germanium recyclers and alternative feedstock processors. The medium-term winners are whoever controls the Oklahoma and Canadian zinc smelter residue streams that represent the only realistic Western production upside. The losers are any company with long-dated fiber procurement contracts written before the export ban — and the satellite operators that depend on their delivery schedules.

title: Special Edition: The SpaceX S-1 Is Live — Here Is What the Numbers Actually Say
subtitle: Starlink at $11.4B revenue. GAAP net loss of $4.9B. Musk controls 79% of votes. The roadshow begins today.
summary: The SpaceX S-1 dropped this morning and the roadshow launches today. After two years of the most-anticipated IPO in history, the actual numbers are finally public. Starlink revenue came in at $11.4B. GAAP net loss of $4.9B — driven almost entirely by Starship development costs. Elon Musk controls 79% of voting power post-IPO. The offering is targeting a $2 trillion valuation at $75 billion raised. Here is a breakdown of what the S-1 actually reveals and what it means for investors at every entry point.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: The SpaceX S-1 is live. The roadshow begins today, June 4, 2026. Pricing is set for June 11. First day of trading on the Nasdaq under ticker SPCX is targeted for June 12. After years of the most-anticipated IPO in modern market history, the actual numbers are finally public — and some of them are not what the headlines are saying.
WHAT THE S-1 ACTUALLY SAYS

Starlink revenue: $11.4 billion. That is the number that matters. Starlink is approximately 69% of total SpaceX revenue, and it is the asset the public market is actually buying. The growth trajectory — from roughly $2B in 2022 to $11.4B — is the steepest revenue ramp of any hardware-dependent consumer service in history, including Netflix's first decade.

GAAP net loss: $4.9 billion. This is the number that will generate the most noise and the least useful analysis. The loss is driven almost entirely by Starship development — R&D that is expensed under GAAP but represents capital investment in what is effectively the world's only reusable super-heavy launch vehicle program. Strip out Starship development costs and the Starlink business is profitable at the operating level.

Voting control: Elon Musk controls 79% of voting power post-IPO through a dual-class share structure. The public offering represents economic exposure to SpaceX's cash flows without meaningful governance rights. This is not unusual for founder-led technology companies at IPO — but it is worth understanding before you allocate capital.

Valuation ask: $2 trillion at $75 billion raised. This prices Starlink at approximately 175x trailing revenue — a multiple that requires you to believe Starlink will be a $50-100B annual revenue business within a decade. The bull case is Direct-to-Cell, maritime, aviation, and enterprise government contracts layered on top of the existing consumer subscriber base. The bear case is that the total addressable market is smaller than the current ask implies.

Investor Consideration: The allocation question is more important than the valuation question for most individual investors. SpaceX has committed to allocating 30% of the offering to retail — at least three times the Wall Street standard. Fidelity, Schwab, and TD Ameritrade accounts are IPO-eligible. The waitlist filled in under 48 hours. If you do not already have an IPO-eligible brokerage account set up, the window for primary allocation is effectively closed.

title: The Valley of Death in Space Insurance — and Who's Filling It
subtitle: The space insurance market absorbed a $995M loss against $557M in premiums in 2023. The fix is arriving from three directions at once.
summary: For decades, space insurance operated as a gentlemen's market — a handful of Lloyd's syndicates, a few specialty underwriters, and a small pool of reinsurance capital covering a small number of high-value GEO satellites. 2023 broke that model: $995M in claims against $557M in premiums, a 179% loss ratio driven by two GEO satellite malfunctions each valued above $400M. Annual premium income still sits around $550-600M. But the infrastructure being built right now — a software startup that became a licensed broker, a Bermuda specialty insurer expanding its product suite, and the world's largest brokerage consolidating under a single brand — will determine who captures the premium volume when mandatory LEO coverage arrives.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: The space insurance market absorbed a $995M loss year in 2023 — nearly double the roughly $557M in premiums collected that year — and the structural fix is now coming from three directions at once: a software startup that became a licensed broker, a Bermuda specialty insurer expanding its product suite, and the world's largest brokerage consolidating under a single brand. Annual premium income in this market still sits around $550-600M (the broader insurance value chain is measured in the billions), so the infrastructure being built right now will determine who captures the premium volume when mandatory LEO coverage arrives.
THE VALLEY OF DEATH IN SPACE INSURANCE — AND WHO'S FILLING IT

For decades, space insurance operated as a gentlemen's market. A handful of Lloyd's syndicates, a few specialty underwriters, and a small pool of reinsurance capital covered a small number of high-value GEO satellites. The economics worked because the assets were large, the clients were few, and the underwriting was manual. Then the rocket equation changed.

The commercial LEO explosion broke that model in two directions simultaneously. On the loss side, 2023 became the worst year in over two decades: total claim payouts reached approximately $995 million against $557 million in premiums collected — a loss ratio of nearly 179% — driven largely by a pair of GEO satellite malfunctions each valued above $400 million. On the demand side, the same period saw LEO satellite deployments accelerate beyond anything the traditional market was designed to cover. The result is a market that has seen its worst loss year on record and its largest structural growth opportunity at exactly the same time.

The traditional Lloyd's model underwrites individual, high-value satellites with bespoke policies negotiated over months. That model does not scale to constellations of 100, 1,000, or 10,000 satellites. It cannot process the actuarial data from a Starlink or OneWeb deployment in the time required to write coverage. The underwriters who will capture the next decade of premium growth are the ones building parametric, data-driven products that can be priced and issued at scale.

Investor Consideration: The total addressable market for space insurance is currently $550-600M in annual premium. Industry projections put that number at $3-5B within a decade as LEO constellations scale and regulatory frameworks in the US, EU, and UK move toward mandatory third-party liability coverage. The companies positioning themselves as the infrastructure layer — brokers, data providers, parametric underwriters — are more interesting than the incumbent syndicates at this stage of the market cycle.

title: A Pharma Company Is Now Paying to Make Drugs in Space
subtitle: United Therapeutics is paying Varda Space Industries to fly its drugs to orbit. Here is why microgravity manufacturing just became a commercial line item.
summary: For two decades, the case for manufacturing in orbit lived almost entirely inside government-funded experiments on the ISS. Companies flew samples, published results, and went home. Nobody was buying a product. That changed this month. United Therapeutics — a Nasdaq-listed maker of treatments for pulmonary arterial hypertension, run by Martine Rothblatt — confirmed it is paying Varda Space Industries to fly its drugs to orbit and search for new crystal forms. The mechanism is genuinely strange and useful: in microgravity, molecules can crystallize into arrangements that are impossible on Earth, changing how a drug dissolves, how long it stores, and how it can be administered.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: For two decades, the case for manufacturing in orbit lived almost entirely inside government-funded experiments on the International Space Station. Companies flew samples, published interesting results, and went home. Nobody was buying a product. The science was real, but the business was a slideshow.
A PHARMA COMPANY IS NOW PAYING TO MAKE DRUGS IN SPACE

That changed this month. United Therapeutics — a Nasdaq-listed maker of treatments for pulmonary arterial hypertension, run by Martine Rothblatt, a satellite industry veteran — confirmed it is paying Varda Space Industries to fly its drugs to orbit and search for new crystal forms. The mechanism is genuinely strange and useful: on Earth, gravity drives convection and sedimentation, forces that distort how a molecule assembles into a solid. Remove gravity and the same drug can crystallize into arrangements — polymorphs — that are purer, more uniform, or simply impossible to make on the ground.

A different crystal form can dissolve differently, store longer, or work as an IV drip instead of an inhaler. For a drugmaker, that is how you extend a franchise and keep imitators at bay for another decade. United Therapeutics' pulmonary arterial hypertension franchise generates over $2B annually. Even a marginal improvement in bioavailability or shelf life — if it qualifies as a new formulation under FDA rules — resets the patent clock.

Varda's business model is the key enabler. The company builds small satellite-based manufacturing platforms — essentially drug factories in a reentry capsule — that go up on a Rocket Lab Electron, spend weeks in microgravity processing a client's materials, and return the product to Earth. The client never needs to understand orbital mechanics. They hand over a compound, Varda handles the mission, and a capsule lands in the Utah desert with a crystallized product inside.

This is the first confirmed commercial transaction in the space manufacturing sector where a company with no space expertise is paying for orbital processing as a line item in its R&D budget. It is not a grant. It is not a government contract. It is a purchase order.

Investor Consideration: Varda is the most interesting pure-play in orbital manufacturing right now. The United Therapeutics deal validates the revenue model — a contract manufacturing organization in orbit that services any industry whose molecules behave differently without gravity. Pharmaceuticals are the beachhead. Semiconductors, fiber optic preforms, and protein crystals for structural biology are the expansion markets. Watch for the Series C announcement.

title: SpaceX Numbers Are Leaking — Here's What We Know Before the S-1 Drops
subtitle: Starlink at $11.4B. GAAP net loss of $4.9B. Musk controls 79% of votes. Here is what the leaked figures mean before the prospectus is official.
summary: The SpaceX S-1 has not dropped yet, but the numbers are leaking. Multiple sources citing the prospectus in circulation among institutional investors put Starlink revenue at $11.4B, total GAAP net loss at $4.9B — driven by Starship development costs — and Musk's post-IPO voting control at 79%. The roadshow launches June 4. Pricing is set for June 11. First day of trading targets June 12 on the Nasdaq under SPCX. Here is what to make of the numbers before they are official.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: The SpaceX S-1 has not been filed yet, but the numbers are in circulation among institutional investors and they are leaking. Here is what multiple sources are reporting ahead of the official prospectus.
WHAT THE LEAKED NUMBERS SAY

Starlink revenue: $11.4 billion. This is the core number. Starlink represents approximately 69% of total SpaceX revenue and is the primary asset the public market will be purchasing. The satellite business — not the launch business — is the investment thesis.

GAAP net loss: $4.9 billion. This figure will generate enormous noise and almost no useful analysis. The loss is a function of how SpaceX accounts for Starship development under US GAAP — expensing as R&D what is effectively capital investment in the only reusable super-heavy launch vehicle program on Earth. The Starlink business itself is operationally profitable.

Voting control: Elon Musk controls 79% of voting power post-IPO through a dual-class share structure. Public shareholders own economic exposure to SpaceX's cash flows without meaningful governance rights. This is structurally identical to how Alphabet, Meta, and Snap went public.

Timeline: The roadshow launches June 4. Pricing is expected June 11. First day of trading is targeted for June 12, 2026, on the Nasdaq under ticker SPCX. The company is targeting a $2 trillion valuation on $75 billion raised — the largest IPO in history by a factor of more than two.

Investor Consideration: The allocation window for retail investors is opening now. SpaceX has committed to allocating 30% of the offering to retail participants — at least three times the industry standard. Fidelity, Schwab, and TD Ameritrade are the primary access points. The IPO-eligible account waitlists are filling rapidly. If you want primary allocation, the setup needs to happen today, not the week of pricing.

title: The SpaceX IPO: The Window, the Math, and the Honest Truth
subtitle: The largest IPO in history is 24 days away. Here is how to position at every capital level — and five public stocks already pricing in the halo.
