author: Orbital Economics

body.content: The largest IPO in history is 24 days away — here is how to position at every capital level, and five public stocks already pricing in the halo.
THE SPACEX IPO: THE WINDOW, THE MATH, AND THE HONEST TRUTH

For two years, the most common question in the Orbital Economics inbox has been some version of: how do I get into SpaceX? That question now has a hard deadline. SpaceX is targeting June 12, 2026, as its first day of trading on the Nasdaq under ticker SPCX. Pricing is expected June 11. The investor roadshow launches June 4. And the public prospectus — the document that will reveal Starlink's actual revenue numbers for the first time — is expected to drop as early as this Wednesday, May 20.

The scale of what is happening is genuinely hard to frame. SpaceX is targeting a $2 trillion valuation on a $75 billion raise. Saudi Aramco held the previous IPO record at $29.4 billion raised. SpaceX is targeting more than twice that. At $2 trillion, it would rank among the six most valuable publicly traded companies on the planet — just below Amazon. At roughly 125 times current revenue, it is pricing in a decade of perfect execution: Starlink growth, Starship commercialization, and the orbital AI computing thesis Elon Musk has been building toward since the xAI merger closed in February.

One detail stands out for individual investors: SpaceX has reportedly committed to allocating 30% of the offering to retail investors — at least three times the Wall Street standard. Even so, demand is expected to massively exceed supply. Getting an allocation through your brokerage will require having an IPO-eligible account set up in advance. Fidelity, Schwab, and TD Ameritrade are the primary access points — the accounts need to be established now.
THE FIVE PUBLIC STOCKS PRICING IN THE HALO

If primary allocation is unavailable, the next question is which public companies move in SpaceX's wake. Five names stand out: Rocket Lab (RKLB) as the clearest beneficiary of renewed investor appetite for pure-play space companies; Planet Labs (PL) as the EO data infrastructure play; Iridium (IRDM) as the LEO communications comparison; Redwire (RDW) as the in-space manufacturing exposure; and Intuitive Machines (LUNR) as the lunar surface logistics proxy.

The honest truth: at 125x revenue, the SpaceX valuation is not a traditional investment analysis. It is a bet on the decade-long trajectory of the space economy — that Starlink becomes the default connectivity layer for aviation, maritime, enterprise, and direct-to-cell mobile; that Starship brings launch costs below $100/kg and opens markets that do not yet exist; and that the orbital AI computing thesis Musk has been articulating becomes a real revenue stream within five years. If you believe those things, the price is not the issue. If you do not, no multiple justifies the entry.

Investor Consideration: The IPO will be the single most-covered financial event of 2026. The halo effect on public space companies will be real but temporary. The more durable opportunity is in the supply chain plays — the companies building the infrastructure that SpaceX, xAI, and every constellation operator will need regardless of whether the IPO prices at $2T or $1.5T.

title: The Golden Dome Supply Chain: Beyond the Obvious Names
subtitle: RTX, LMT, NOC are the right names. They are also the fully-priced names. Here is where capital can still move ahead of the market.
summary: Twenty posts in, the investment thesis at the center of this newsletter — that space infrastructure is the defining capital allocation story of this decade — just received its largest single policy validation. Golden Dome is not just a defense program. It is a $185 billion procurement cycle with 2,440 approved vendors and a four-year deadline. The primes are obvious. Here are the plays nobody is talking about: the five constraint sub-tiers that an independent AIA/PwC study identified as Golden Dome's most likely schedule bottlenecks — optical inter-satellite link terminals, radiation-hardened electronics, EO/IR sensors, solid rocket motors, and GaN RF components.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: Twenty posts in, the investment thesis at the center of this newsletter — that space infrastructure is the defining capital allocation story of this decade — just received its largest single policy validation.
THE GOLDEN DOME SUPPLY CHAIN: BEYOND THE OBVIOUS NAMES

RTX, LMT, NOC. If you have read any coverage of Golden Dome this week, you have seen those three tickers in every headline. They are the right names. They are also the fully-priced names. The more interesting question is where capital can still move ahead of the market — in the supply chain tiers that have to scale whether or not any single prime wins the next contract.

An independent AIA/PwC study from March 2026 identified five component sub-tiers as Golden Dome's most likely schedule constraints: optical inter-satellite link terminals, radiation-hardened electronics, EO/IR sensors, solid rocket motors, and GaN RF components. Two of these already have documented production capacity gaps. Programs like this don't stall because a prime fails a design review. They stall because a program is three tiers below ran out of a specific grade of gallium nitride substrate.

Golden Dome is not just a defense program. It is a $185 billion procurement cycle with 2,440 approved vendors and a four-year deadline. The program architecture requires a proliferated LEO constellation for midcourse tracking — satellites that need optical ISL terminals to communicate with each other without routing through ground stations. Current US production capacity for space-qualified optical ISL terminals is a fraction of what the program requires. The companies that can scale that capacity are not household names.

The radiation-hardened electronics constraint is equally acute. Rad-hard processors, memory, and power management ICs are produced by a small number of qualified fabs — primarily Microchip Technology, BAE Systems, and a handful of European suppliers. Golden Dome's sensor layer requires rad-hard components in quantities that current qualified production lines cannot deliver on a four-year timeline without significant capacity expansion.

Investor Consideration: The obvious primes — RTX, LMT, NOC, L3Harris — are priced for Golden Dome. The supply chain plays are not. Look at the second and third-tier suppliers in optical ISL, rad-hard semiconductors, and GaN RF. These companies will see demand that their current market caps do not reflect. The constraint is not capital — it is qualified production capacity, and that takes time to build. The window to get positioned ahead of that realization is the next 90 days.

title: When the Sky Became the Front Line
subtitle: Operation Epic Fury battle-tested commercial EO satellites in real-time warfare. Capital is now repricing the entire sector.
summary: Israeli officials described Operation Roaring Lion as the first conflict in history where commercial satellites played a decisive role from start to finish. SAR satellites from ICEYE and Umbra delivered 24/7 visibility through dust and smoke. The battle-testing that defense agencies once required over years happened in a single week. This post maps how capital is repricing the EO stack — from SkyFi’s asset-light marketplace to Northwood’s ground infrastructure, plus Planet Labs’ SHIELD prime contract and SpaceX’s IPO timeline.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: Israeli officials described Operation Roaring Lion as the first conflict in history where commercial satellites played a decisive role from start to finish. The US-Israeli strikes that began February 28 — codenamed Operation Epic Fury by CENTCOM — turned commercial Earth observation into live wartime infrastructure. SAR satellites from companies like ICEYE and Umbra delivered 24/7 visibility through dust and smoke. The battle-testing that defense agencies once required over years happened in a single week. Capital that was already moving toward this sector just got a very loud green light.
Lead Story: SkyFi — Series A, $12.7M, January 2026

SkyFi does not own a single satellite. It built the marketplace where anyone — a government analyst, an insurance underwriter, a hedge fund, a Reuters photo editor — can order high-resolution Earth imagery on demand, in minutes, with no annual contract required. The platform aggregates over 50 providers including Vantor, Planet Labs, ICEYE, Umbra, Satellogic, and Airbus Pléiades Neo. Pick a location, select a provider and resolution, and imagery arrives — including direct delivery to AWS S3 for enterprise workflows.

The Iran conflict put SkyFi in front of the world without a marketing dollar spent. OSINT analyst Brady Africk used the platform to publish annotated Satellogic imagery of the compound where the supreme leader was killed — shared globally within hours of capture. Vantor imagery of Natanz and Konarak Naval Base ran simultaneously on CNN, NPR, the New York Times, and Reuters. CEO Luke Fischer said the bottleneck is not getting imagery; it is getting answers. The company’s next build is AI-driven analytics that deliver intelligence, not pixels.

Investor Consideration: Asset-light model with strong gross margin potential at scale. The March 2026 conflict is the most powerful unplanned product demonstration in the company’s history. Defense and intelligence contract pipeline opened dramatically in one week. Series B likely late 2026 — watch for it.
Planet Labs (NYSE: PL) — SHIELD Prime Contract

Planet operates the world’s largest Earth observation constellation, and its imagery defined global understanding of the Iran strikes. On March 3rd the company was named a prime contractor under the Missile Defense Agency’s SHIELD IDIQ — a vehicle with up to a $151 billion ceiling shared across multiple primes. Planet’s backlog grew 216% year-over-year to $734M, with approximately 27% full-year revenue growth guidance for fiscal 2026. Next-generation Pelican satellites carry Nvidia Jetson AI chips for onboard processing.
Northwood Space — Series B, $100M, January 2026

Every satellite in orbit needs to talk to Earth, and Northwood builds the modern ground infrastructure that makes that possible. The Series B was led by Washington Harbour Partners and co-led by Andreessen Horowitz. Northwood secured a $49.8M Space Force contract to modernize the Satellite Control Network — replacing 1970s-era dishes with phased-array Portals that handle classified government space missions. Targeting deployment across five continents by end of 2026.
Orbitworks — Abu Dhabi’s First Satellite Factory

The Middle East’s first private satellite manufacturing facility is now operational in Abu Dhabi — a joint venture between Marlan Space (backed by International Holding Company) and US-based Loft Orbital. Initial investment exceeds $100M, targeting production of up to 50 satellites per year at 500kg class. The Gulf states just watched commercial satellites document Iranian strikes on their neighbors in real time. Sovereign EO demand in the region will not decrease.
Vantor — From Maxar to War’s Most-Published Imagery

Vantor’s 0.3-meter optical satellites produced imagery of Khamenei’s compound, the Natanz enrichment facility, Konarak Naval Base, and Tehran Air Force Command headquarters — published by CBS, NPR, CNN, and Reuters simultaneously. Vantor emerged from Advent International’s 2023 acquisition of Maxar Technologies, rebranded in October 2025 alongside manufacturing spinout Lanteris. The company distributes commercially through SkyFi’s platform and fuses satellite data with air and ground sensor networks as a unified spatial intelligence system.
SpaceX — IPO Watch

Elon Musk confirmed in December 2025 that a SpaceX IPO is planned for 2026. In February 2026, SpaceX formally acquired xAI in an all-stock deal, combining Starlink broadband, Grok AI, and SpaceX’s launch infrastructure at a combined private valuation of approximately $1.25 trillion. Multiple financial outlets cite mid-2026 as the most likely window, at a target valuation of $1.5 trillion. Starlink reached 9.2 million subscribers at end-2025, roughly 69% of SpaceX revenue. No S-1 has been filed. Wait for the filing.

title: He³ in Lunar Permanently Shadowed Regions: Concentrations, Mechanisms, and Resource Implications
subtitle: A literature synthesis on Helium-3 cold-trapping in polar craters and what it means for ISRU planning
summary: Permanently shadowed regions at the lunar poles may contain He³ concentrations 3–10x higher than sunlit mare soil. This working paper synthesizes the primary research — from Cocks (2010) PSR estimates to NASA's own 2021 engineering baseline — and evaluates what the data actually supports for mission architecture and extraction planning.
author: Vlad Algin

body.content: Scope Note: This document is a synthesis and review of publicly available scientific literature on He³ concentrations in lunar permanently shadowed regions (PSRs). It does not present original experimental data. All findings are attributed to their primary sources with verified citations. The author's contribution is the selection, analysis, cross-verification, and synthesis of the material presented.
Overview

Permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) — polar craters that never receive direct sunlight — are theorized to contain significantly elevated concentrations of Helium-3 (He³) compared to sunlit lunar surfaces. In sunlit areas, measured He³ concentrations in Apollo and Luna sample returns range from 1.4 to 15 ppb, with higher values found in titanium-rich mare regions. In PSRs, cryogenic temperatures are estimated to enable concentrations of up to 50 ppb or more. Crucially, the PSR estimate is a theoretical projection — no in-situ measurement has been made.
Mechanisms of Concentration

Research distinguishes two populations of He³ in the regolith. Strongly bound helium is implanted by the solar wind into crystal lattice vacancies of minerals — primarily ilmenite (FeTiO₃), which has a high concentration of radiation-induced defects that effectively trap solar wind ions. This component has a high activation energy and requires heating to approximately 700°C for full release.

Weakly bound (inter-grained) helium sits between mineral grains. This component is highly temperature-sensitive: diurnal heating in sunlit regions causes this weakly bound He³ to desorb and escape to the exosphere. Studies confirm that the spatial variability of He³ retention is strongly controlled by surface temperature.
Thermal Retention in PSRs

PSRs are the coldest places in the solar system. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Diviner instrument recorded surface temperatures as low as 20 K in south polar craters, with a general PSR temperature range of approximately 20–70 K. (Note: 110 K is the threshold temperature at which PSRs are generally defined as cold traps for water ice stability; actual crater floor temperatures are substantially colder.) These cryogenic conditions prevent the thermal desorption of weakly bound He³, enabling accumulation over geological time.
Migration and Cold-Trapping Hypothesis

It is hypothesized that He³ atoms liberated from warmer sunlit regolith can migrate ballistically across the lunar surface and become cold-trapped upon entering a PSR — analogous to the mechanism by which water ice accumulates in these craters. This migration-and-trapping model is consistent with the broader volatile cold-trap literature but, like the elevated concentration estimates themselves, awaits direct ground-truth verification.
Key Research and Concentration Estimates

Cocks, F.H. (2010) in Icarus 206 provides the primary source for the PSR cold-trap concentration estimate of 50 ppb+, modeling cryogenic accumulation in polar craters. Apollo sample databases show 1.4–15 ppb from direct measurements of returned regolith in sunlit areas. Kim et al. (2019) mapped global distribution with maximum ~20 ppb in sunlit titanium-rich maria, confirming temperature-dependent retention. Olson et al. (2021) from NASA NTRS provides an engineering feasibility baseline at 20 ppb — notably assuming PSR concentrations similar to equatorial, with the PSR premium not yet incorporated into NASA mission planning.
Comparative Concentration Summary

Equatorial Maria (Ti-rich): Up to ~20 ppb, retained through mineral-bound ilmenite with high solar wind flux. Highlands: 1–4 ppb due to low titanium content and poor mineral retention. Polar Craters (PSRs): Up to ~50 ppb (theoretical), retained through cryogenic cold-trapping at 20–70 K with no diurnal degassing. This last figure remains unverified by in-situ measurement.
Key Caveats for Planning Purposes

Source accuracy: The 50 ppb PSR figure originates from Cocks (2010) — a theoretical model, not a direct measurement. No sample return or landed mission has yet measured He³ in a PSR. NASA baseline: NASA's own 2021 engineering feasibility paper assumes PSR He³ concentrations are similar to equatorial regions — the premium has not been incorporated into mission architecture planning.

Temperature range: PSR temperatures are 20–70 K, not 50–100 K as sometimes stated. This is relevant to hardware survival and power budgeting for extraction equipment. Extraction trade-off: The equatorial maria (Mare Tranquillitatis, Oceanus Procellarum) remain the highest-confidence targets for near-term He³ extraction due to validated titanium-ilmenite concentrations and accessible terrain.

Extraction energy: The weakly bound inter-grained He³ in PSRs may require lower extraction temperatures than ilmenite-bound equatorial He³ (~700°C), but operating at 20–70 K introduces severe power and hardware durability constraints.
Verified Citations

Primary sources: [1] Wikipedia / Apollo sample database (He³ lunar concentrations). [2] Fa & Jin (2007), Icarus 190 — Quantitative estimation of He³ spatial distribution. [3] Cocks (2010), Icarus 206 — He³ in permanently shadowed lunar surfaces. [4] Kim et al. (2019), Planet. Space Sci. 177 — He³-rich landing sites. [5] Olson (2021), NASA NTRS — He³ mining concepts and ISRU synergies. [6] Bhatt et al. (2020), Remote Sensing 12(20) — Solar wind He³ retention analysis. [7] Siegler et al. (2016), Nature — Lunar true polar wander. [8] Wikipedia — Permanently shadowed crater (LRO Diviner data). [9] Arnold (1979), JGR 84(B10) — Ice in lunar polar regions. [10] Slyuta et al. (2007), LPSC Abstract 2175. [11] Bickel et al. (2021), Nature Comms. 12 — Deep learning PSR imaging.

title: Golden Dome's Hidden Supply Chain: Where Tier-2 Capital Is Actually Moving
subtitle: Mapping the tier-2 manufacturers whose components the primes cannot build fast enough at scale
summary: Everyone is watching Anduril, Lockheed, and SpaceX position for Golden Dome. The $151B SHIELD contract vehicle now has 2,100 qualifying vendors. This post maps the layer most investors aren't watching yet: the tier-2 manufacturers — from Apex Space's satellite buses to AST SpaceMobile's defense broadband — whose components the primes cannot build fast enough at scale.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: Everyone is watching Anduril, Lockheed, and SpaceX position for Golden Dome. The $151B SHIELD contract vehicle now has 2,100 qualifying vendors. The FY2026 defense bill signed February 3 allocated $13.4B specifically for space and missile defense. Congress has given the Pentagon 60 days to produce a public spend plan. When that plan lands — likely late March or April — it will identify which supply chain categories receive priority capital. The post below maps the layer most investors aren't watching yet: the tier-2 manufacturers whose components the primes cannot build fast enough at scale.
Lead Story: Apex Space — The Satellite Bus That Became an Arsenal
Los Angeles, CA | Founded 2022 | $400M+ raised | Valuation: $1B+

Apex doesn't build interceptors. It builds the platform that carries them — and that distinction may matter more than any individual weapons contract. The company has completed two $200M funding rounds in consecutive quarters and is now the de facto mass-manufacturer of configurable satellite buses for defense constellations. Its three platforms — Aries, Nova, and Comet — carry 100 to 500 kg of payload. In their heavier Orbital Magazine configuration, the Nova and Comet can host 1,000 kg and 5,000 kg of interceptor payload respectively. A new factory is already equipped to produce 200+ satellites per year.

For Golden Dome, the Nova bus is the host for Project Shadow: a self-funded, $15M in-orbit demonstration of an "Orbital Magazine" — a spacecraft that stores, thermally controls, and deploys kinetic interceptors on command. Launch is scheduled for NET June 2026. The spacecraft uses a software-defined radio transmitting Link-182 messages — the exact data link standard the U.S. Space Force has adopted for MILNET, its future low-Earth orbit communications relay network. Apex is pre-integrating into the DoD architecture before that architecture is fully defined.

The Pentagon doesn't need one demonstration. It needs thousands of satellite buses, produced at commercial rates, to field a viable constellation. Apex has also announced a strategic partnership with Anduril to supply buses for Anduril's defense payloads — a tier-1-to-tier-2 supply relationship forming in public view.

Investor Consideration: Pre-IPO at $1B+ valuation. June 2026 Project Shadow launch is the nearest public milestone. Factory scale-up trajectory and the Anduril partnership signal that contract pipeline is forming ahead of formal Golden Dome awards.
Voyager Technologies (NYSE: VOYG) — Defense & Space Infrastructure
Denver, CO | Public June 2025

Voyager is currently the only publicly traded pure-play in this tier-2 supply chain, making it the most visible benchmark for the sector. In October 2025, Voyager acquired ExoTerra Resource, a developer of high-efficiency electric propulsion systems enabling precise spacecraft maneuvering — a critical capability for any constellation that needs to reposition, avoid threats, or sustain mission advantage. In January 2026, Voyager secured a patent for producing ultra-pure optical crystals in microgravity, with ISS validation flights planned for spring 2026. The stock is currently trading around $25.58, roughly 41% below analyst consensus target, after a 30-day pullback.

Investor Consideration: Public, liquid, and executing across multiple Golden Dome-adjacent categories. Key 2026 watch: NASA Phase 2 Commercial Low-Earth Orbit Destination (CLD) award — a contract win could be transformative; a miss would pressure the balance sheet.
True Anomaly — Autonomous Orbital Vehicles + Space Domain Awareness
Centennial, CO | $389M raised | Series C led by Accel

True Anomaly builds two interlocking products: the Jackal autonomous orbital vehicle, which can maneuver, track, and operate against threats on orbit; and Mosaic, the AI-driven software operating system for space domain awareness. The company was awarded a $30M Space Force contract for the VICTUS HAZE mission — a tactically responsive space demonstration alongside Firefly Aerospace. In November 2025, True Anomaly was among 18 companies awarded classified OTA contracts for boost-phase space-based interceptor prototypes; its name has since surfaced publicly. Jackal and Mosaic are both scheduled for their first independent missions to GEO and cislunar space in 2026.

Investor Consideration: Pre-IPO, $389M raised, active government contracts. SVP Stephen Kitay — former Pentagon space policy lead — has been publicly positioning the company against the 2026 National Defense Strategy, a signal of deliberate contract pipeline development.
Portal Space Systems — Solar Thermal Propulsion
Redmond, WA | Early stage

Portal is developing the Afterburner, a solar thermal propulsion system that uses concentrated sunlight to superheat propellant — delivering higher specific impulse than chemical thrusters at a fraction of the cost. The problem it solves: a maneuverable Golden Dome constellation requires spacecraft that can reposition and persist without burning through chemical propellant budgets. Portal's approach makes sustained, responsive maneuvering economically viable. The company is based in Redmond, WA, inside the same aerospace corridor as Blue Origin and Boeing's space programs, and has received early-stage government interest.

Investor Consideration: Early stage, no public funding round disclosed. Payload Space's 2025 Golden Dome supply chain review flagged Portal as a company to watch. A Series A announcement in 2026 would be the catalyst to track.
Quantum Space — Cislunar Situational Awareness + Relay Infrastructure
Columbia, MD | Draper Laboratory-backed

Quantum Space began as a cislunar relay play — positioning communications and navigation nodes beyond GEO to support lunar missions. Its pivot toward Golden Dome is more recent but logical: any SBI constellation that needs to cover ICBM boost phases over polar routes will eventually require sensor and relay architecture in the cislunar environment. Quantum Space's Eos spacecraft program has drawn U.S. Space Force interest, and the Draper Laboratory backing provides deep institutional credibility in defense-adjacent navigation and guidance systems.

Investor Consideration: Draper-backed, Space Force interest confirmed. As Golden Dome architecture discussions expand beyond LEO, cislunar-capable companies gain strategic relevance. No public funding round yet — watch for one in 2026.
AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ: ASTS) — Space-Based Cellular Connectivity
Midland, TX | Public | Market cap ~$4B

AST SpaceMobile is building the first space-based cellular broadband network capable of connecting standard smartphones directly from orbit — no specialized hardware required. The relevance to Golden Dome: the DoD has now awarded AST SpaceMobile a prime contract position on U.S. missile defense infrastructure, recognizing its direct-to-device broadband capability as a resilient communications layer for defense operations. The company launched its first commercial BlueBird satellites in 2024 and is scaling the constellation aggressively through 2026.

Investor Consideration: Publicly traded, liquid, and now formally integrated into missile defense architecture. The DoD contract represents a material shift in how AST's addressable market is understood — from commercial carrier play to dual-use defense infrastructure.
The Signal: Watch for the Spend Plan

The SHIELD IDIQ mechanism means qualifying vendors can receive task orders without new sole-source justifications or full competitive re-bids — that's not how defense contracting normally works. Congress has now demanded Gen. Guetlein's office publish a comprehensive spend plan within 60 days of the February 3 bill signing. When that plan becomes public — likely late March or April 2026 — it will be the clearest signal yet of which tier-2 supply chain categories are being prioritized. That document is the next issue to watch.

title: The Real Cost of Getting to Orbit in 2026
subtitle: A comprehensive breakdown of per-kilogram launch costs across all active providers
summary: A deep analysis of per-kilogram launch costs across all active providers, from SpaceX Falcon 9 ($3,063/kg) to Rocket Lab Electron ($19,231/kg). We break down why Starship could push costs below $500/kg and what that means for commercial satellite operators, university CubeSat programs, and defense payloads.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: The cost of reaching orbit has never been lower — but it's still far from cheap. In 2026, commercial launch costs range from roughly $3,000 to $20,000 per kilogram depending on the vehicle, orbit, and mission profile. Understanding these numbers is critical for anyone planning a satellite deployment, research mission, or constellation build-out.
Current Per-Kilogram Pricing by Provider

SpaceX Falcon 9 remains the benchmark at approximately $3,063/kg to LEO for a dedicated mission. Rideshare slots on Transporter missions can reduce this further for small payloads. ULA's Vulcan Centaur enters the market at roughly $7,500/kg, offering higher-energy orbits and government-grade reliability. Rocket Lab's Electron, designed for dedicated small-sat launches, comes in at around $19,231/kg — a premium justified by precise orbital insertion and rapid scheduling.
The Starship Factor

SpaceX's Starship promises to fundamentally reshape launch economics. With a projected cost below $500/kg to LEO at full reusability, Starship would reduce launch costs by an order of magnitude. This isn't just a pricing shift — it changes satellite design philosophy. When launch is cheap, satellites can be heavier, use less expensive components, and be replaced more frequently.
What This Means for Different Customers

For commercial constellation operators like those building broadband networks, lower costs mean denser satellite meshes and faster deployment timelines. For university CubeSat programs, rideshare missions already make space accessible at $300K-$1M per launch opportunity. For defense and national security payloads, the equation balances cost against assured access, schedule reliability, and orbit flexibility — areas where ULA and Arianespace maintain strong positions.
Key Takeaway

The launch market in 2026 offers more options at more price points than ever before. The right choice depends on your payload mass, target orbit, schedule flexibility, and risk tolerance. Use our calculator to model scenarios with real provider data and find the optimal launch solution for your mission.

title: LEO vs GEO vs MEO: Choosing the Right Orbit for Your Mission
subtitle: A practical comparison of orbital regimes for mission planners
summary: Each orbit type serves different purposes and comes with vastly different costs. LEO (200-2,000 km) is ideal for Earth observation and broadband constellations. GEO (35,786 km) provides fixed coverage for communications. MEO sits between them for navigation. We compare delta-v requirements, launch costs, and mission profiles for each.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: Choosing the right orbit is one of the most consequential decisions in mission planning. It determines your launch cost, available rockets, ground coverage pattern, communication latency, radiation environment, and satellite lifetime. This guide breaks down the three primary orbital regimes and when each makes sense.
Low Earth Orbit (LEO): 200–2,000 km

LEO is the most accessible and affordable orbit. Delta-v requirements are approximately 9.4 km/s from Earth's surface, and nearly every operational launch vehicle can reach it. LEO is the domain of the International Space Station, Earth observation satellites, and mega-constellations like Starlink and OneWeb. The tradeoff: LEO satellites move quickly relative to the ground, requiring large constellations for continuous coverage and more complex ground station networks.
Medium Earth Orbit (MEO): 2,000–35,786 km

MEO occupies the space between LEO and GEO. It's primarily used for navigation constellations — GPS (USA), Galileo (EU), GLONASS (Russia), and BeiDou (China) all operate in MEO. The higher altitude means each satellite covers a larger ground footprint, requiring fewer satellites for global coverage than LEO but introducing higher latency than GEO. MEO missions cost more than LEO due to increased delta-v requirements and longer transfer times.
Geostationary Orbit (GEO): 35,786 km

GEO is unique: satellites at this altitude orbit at the same rate Earth rotates, appearing to hover over a fixed point on the equator. This makes GEO ideal for communications satellites, weather monitoring, and military early-warning systems. The delta-v requirement is approximately 14 km/s, significantly more than LEO, which limits the number of vehicles capable of GEO insertion and increases per-kilogram costs substantially.
Cost and Vehicle Comparison

A Falcon 9 can deliver 22,800 kg to LEO but only 8,300 kg to GTO (the transfer orbit for GEO). This capacity reduction directly translates to higher per-kilogram costs for GEO missions. When planning your mission, consider not just the launch cost but the total cost of operations — including ground infrastructure, communication links, and replacement schedules. Our mission planner models these tradeoffs with real provider data.

title: CubeSat Launch Programs: A University Buyer's Guide
subtitle: Everything academic institutions need to know about getting a satellite to orbit
summary: Universities and research institutions are launching more satellites than ever. This guide covers the full lifecycle: from building a 1U-6U CubeSat to selecting a rideshare provider, navigating regulatory approval, and managing mission operations. Includes cost breakdowns, timeline expectations, and provider comparisons.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: Academic satellite programs have exploded in the past decade. What once required national space agency backing can now be accomplished by a university lab with a modest budget and a two-year timeline. CubeSats — standardized small satellites measured in 10cm units (1U = 10×10×10 cm) — have democratized access to space for research and education.
Understanding CubeSat Form Factors

CubeSats range from 1U (1.33 kg) to 12U and beyond. For university programs, 1U to 6U is most common. A 1U CubeSat is sufficient for simple technology demonstrations and basic Earth imaging. 3U provides room for more capable payloads including better optics, communication experiments, and scientific instruments. 6U is becoming the standard for serious research missions, offering enough volume and mass budget for meaningful scientific returns.
Launch Options and Costs

Rideshare missions are the most cost-effective path to orbit for CubeSats. SpaceX's Transporter rideshare missions offer slots starting around $275K for a 1U deployer. Rocket Lab offers dedicated missions with precise orbital insertion at higher per-kg cost but with the advantage of choosing your exact orbit. ISRO's PSLV also provides competitive rideshare pricing for academic payloads. Total mission costs (satellite build + launch + operations) typically range from $500K for a simple 1U to $3M+ for a capable 6U mission.
Regulatory Requirements

In the United States, CubeSat missions require FCC licensing for radio frequency use and FAA licensing for launch. Universities must also register with the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs through their national space agency. The licensing process typically takes 6-12 months, so it should begin well before your launch window. International programs face similar requirements through their national regulatory bodies.
Timeline and Planning

A realistic timeline from program start to launch is 18-36 months. This includes satellite design and build (8-18 months), environmental testing (2-3 months), regulatory licensing (6-12 months, often in parallel), launch integration (1-3 months), and early operations (1-3 months). Use our mission planning tools to model costs and timelines based on your specific payload requirements.

title: SpaceX Starship: What $500/kg to LEO Means for the Industry
subtitle: Modeling the downstream effects of dramatically lower launch costs
summary: Starship's promised cost reduction isn't just a number — it's a paradigm shift. We model the downstream effects on satellite design (heavier, cheaper components), constellation economics (larger, denser networks), and the competitive landscape for legacy providers like ULA, Arianespace, and Roscosmos.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: When SpaceX achieves full Starship reusability with rapid turnaround, the launch industry faces its most significant disruption since the introduction of reusable first stages. At a projected $500/kg to LEO — compared to the current Falcon 9 benchmark of $3,063/kg — the economics of space change fundamentally.
Satellite Design Revolution

Today's satellites are engineered to be as light as possible because every kilogram costs thousands of dollars to launch. At $500/kg, mass constraints relax dramatically. Satellite manufacturers can use heavier, cheaper, more readily available components instead of space-grade minimized versions. This reduces satellite build costs and shortens production timelines. The result: cheaper, faster-to-build satellites that can be replaced more frequently.
Constellation Economics

Starship's massive payload capacity (100-150 tonnes to LEO) combined with low per-kg costs makes ultra-large constellations economically viable. Instead of 1,000-satellite networks, operators could deploy 10,000+ satellites for denser coverage, lower latency, and more redundancy. This changes the business model for broadband, IoT, and Earth observation services.
Competitive Pressure on Legacy Providers

ULA, Arianespace, and Roscosmos face existential competitive pressure. ULA's Vulcan Centaur at ~$7,500/kg and Ariane 6 at similar price points cannot compete on cost alone. These providers must differentiate on reliability, orbit capability, government relationships, and assured access mandates. Roscosmos, already struggling with sanctions and aging infrastructure, faces the steepest challenge.
Timeline and Reality Check

The $500/kg target assumes full and rapid reusability of both stages plus the payload fairing, high launch cadence, and mature operations. As of early 2026, Starship has completed several test flights with increasing success, but operational commercial service with full reusability remains ahead. The trajectory is clear, but the timeline is uncertain. Smart operators are planning for a range of scenarios.

title: Space Insurance 101: Protecting Your Payload Investment
subtitle: Understanding premiums, coverage, and how to reduce launch insurance costs
summary: Launch insurance premiums typically run 5-15% of the total mission value. We explain the underwriting process, what policies cover (launch failure, in-orbit anomalies, third-party liability), and how to reduce premiums. Includes data on historical claim rates by provider and vehicle type.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: Space insurance is a specialized but essential component of mission planning. With satellite values ranging from $5M for a small commercial bird to $500M+ for major government systems, protecting that investment against launch failure or in-orbit anomalies is a critical financial decision. Understanding how the space insurance market works can save you significant costs.
Types of Space Insurance

There are four main categories: Pre-launch insurance covers the satellite during manufacturing and transport. Launch insurance covers from ignition through orbit insertion. In-orbit insurance covers the satellite during its operational life. Third-party liability insurance covers damage to other assets or people. Most commercial missions carry launch insurance at minimum, with premiums typically ranging from 5-15% of the insured value.
How Premiums Are Calculated

Underwriters assess several factors: the launch vehicle's historical success rate, the complexity of the mission (simple LEO vs. complex GTO insertion), the satellite's design heritage, the insured value, and current market conditions. A Falcon 9 launch, with a 98%+ success rate, typically commands lower premiums than a newer vehicle with less flight heritage. Launch vehicle track record is the single largest factor in premium calculation.
Reducing Your Premiums

Several strategies can lower insurance costs: choosing a vehicle with extensive flight heritage, accepting higher deductibles, insuring for replacement cost rather than new value, demonstrating satellite design heritage through prior successful missions, and maintaining strong quality assurance documentation. For constellation operators launching multiple identical satellites, portfolio approaches and self-insurance on later units can significantly reduce per-satellite insurance costs.
Market Trends

The space insurance market has become more competitive as launch reliability has improved. Premiums have trended downward from historical rates of 15-25% to current rates of 5-12% for established vehicles. However, the market remains cyclical — a major loss event (satellite failure, launch anomaly) can tighten capacity and push rates higher across the industry. Our mission planning tools include insurance estimation based on current market conditions.

title: Rocket Lab vs SpaceX: Small Sat Economics Compared
subtitle: Dedicated launch vs rideshare — which path is right for your payload?
summary: Dedicated vs rideshare: which path makes sense for your payload? Rocket Lab's Electron offers precise orbital insertion for small payloads at a premium, while SpaceX's Transporter rideshare missions offer the lowest per-kg cost but less flexibility. We analyze schedule reliability, integration timelines, and total mission cost.
author: Orbital Economics

body.content: For payloads under 300 kg, two launch approaches dominate the market: Rocket Lab's dedicated Electron missions and SpaceX's Transporter rideshare program. Each offers distinct advantages, and choosing between them depends on your mission requirements, budget, and timeline flexibility. This analysis provides a direct comparison to help inform that decision.
Rocket Lab Electron: The Dedicated Approach

Electron is purpose-built for small payloads up to 300 kg to LEO. At approximately $7.5M per mission ($19,231/kg at max capacity), Electron costs significantly more per kilogram than a rideshare slot. But you get something invaluable: your own rocket. This means precise orbital insertion (exact altitude, inclination, and LTAN), your preferred launch window, and no dependency on a primary payload's schedule. For missions where orbit precision is critical — Earth observation with specific lighting requirements, for example — Electron's premium is justified.
SpaceX Transporter: The Rideshare Value Play

SpaceX's Transporter rideshare missions offer the lowest per-kilogram cost for small satellites, with slots starting around $5,500/kg. These missions typically deploy dozens of satellites into sun-synchronous LEO. The tradeoff: you share the ride with many other payloads, the orbit is predetermined, and scheduling depends on SpaceX's Transporter cadence (roughly quarterly in 2026). If your mission can tolerate a specific orbit and flexible timing, rideshare economics are hard to beat.
Schedule Reliability and Integration

Rocket Lab has demonstrated strong schedule reliability with launch campaigns as short as a few weeks between missions. Integration timelines are typically 4-8 weeks. SpaceX Transporter missions require earlier payload commitment (3-6 months) and have fixed launch dates that occasionally slip. However, SpaceX's high launch cadence means delays rarely push more than a few weeks.
The Decision Framework

Choose Rocket Lab Electron when: orbit precision is critical, you need a specific launch window, your payload requires unique deployment conditions, or you have a time-sensitive mission. Choose SpaceX Transporter when: cost is the primary driver, sun-synchronous LEO is acceptable, schedule flexibility exists, or you're deploying a constellation where exact orbit parameters can be standardized. Many operators use both: Transporter for routine constellation replenishment and Electron for specialty deployments. Use our calculator to compare total mission costs across both providers.
